Chapter 8: The Ongoing Necessity of Resistance
Wouldn’t it be nice if the hard work was over? If we could finally say the world is as fair as it’s ever going to be?
But let’s be honest—the reminders that the fight isn’t finished are everywhere. The forces that push back against change? They’re not just stubborn, they’re clever. They know all the tricks—how to rebrand old ideas with fresh words, or make you feel like the status quo is just how things have to be.
Picture this: there’s a teacher in a small town, trying her best to bring new books into the classroom. She wants her students to see themselves reflected in stories, to learn about lives that aren’t just like their own. But every time she tries to move forward, she gets resistance—from parents, from school leaders, even from neighbors. They tell her to stick with “the classics,” to steer clear of anything “controversial.” The message? Don’t rock the boat.
Here’s the thing: resistance doesn’t always look like rallies or big, dramatic showdowns. Most of the time, it’s about the small, everyday decisions—to tell the truth, to keep paying attention, to keep pushing even when it feels tough. It’s the parent who speaks up at a school board meeting. The worker who starts organizing for better conditions. Or just a friend who decides not to laugh along with a mean-spirited joke.
A lot of us want to believe things will just get better on their own. But let’s face it—progress only happens because someone refuses to settle for less. The people who benefit from the way things are? They’ll always find new ways to protect their position. They’ll call for “civility,” for “patience,” for “understanding”—anything to slow things down or keep change at bay.
That’s why resistance matters, even when it’s exhausting. It’s what leaves the door open for those who’ll come after us. It lets people imagine something better. The work? It’s never really finished. But that doesn’t mean it isn’t worth it.
Sometimes, resistance shows up as anger. Other times, it looks like hope. Most often, it’s just ordinary folks refusing to give in. That’s how real change happens—not in some sudden rush, but because people keep saying “no” to what’s unacceptable, over and over again.
